title: At the Feast of Tabernacles: Living Water
summary: Jesus' brothers urge him to show himself at the Feast of Tabernacles in Jerusalem, but he goes up privately and then teaches openly in the temple courts halfway through the feast. The crowds are divided over whether he is a good man, a deceiver, the Prophet, or the Christ, and the chief priests and Pharisees send officers to arrest him. On the last great day of the feast he invites the thirsty to come to him and drink, and the officers return empty-handed, saying no one ever spoke like this man, while Nicodemus asks in vain for a fair hearing.
story:
The hostility that began in chapter 5 now shapes Jesus' movements. He stays in Galilee because the Judean authorities want him dead (7:1), and chapters 7 and 8 together record a long, tense visit to Jerusalem at the autumn festival, some six months after the Passover of chapter 6. Chapters 5 to 10 follow Israel's feasts, a Sabbath (5), Passover (6), Tabernacles (7 to 9), and Dedication (10), and in each Jesus shows himself to be what the feast celebrates. Here the feast of water and light becomes the setting for his offer of living water (7:37-39) and, in the next chapter, his claim to be the light of the world (8:12).

Throughout the chapter the question is who Jesus is and where he comes from, and every group gives a different answer: his brothers, the crowds, the people of Jerusalem, the Pharisees, the temple officers, and Nicodemus. Chapter 5's healing on the Sabbath is still being argued over (7:21-23). The phrase “My time has not yet come” (7:6) and the note that “His hour had not yet come” (7:30) keep the reader aware that Jesus is moving toward an appointed hour, the hour of his death and glory, which no arrest can bring forward. Nicodemus, who came by night in chapter 3, reappears on the edge of the council, and will appear again at the burial (19:39).
historical:
Religious authority in Jerusalem rested with the high priest (Caiaphas held the office from about AD 18 to 36; Josephus, Antiquities 18.35, 18.95) and the leading priestly families, called in the Gospels the chief priests. Many of them belonged to the Sadducees, an aristocratic party centered on the temple. The Pharisees were a lay movement of teachers devoted to the careful keeping of the law, including traditions of interpretation that later fed into rabbinic Judaism; Josephus says they had great influence with ordinary people (Antiquities 18.15). Both groups were represented on the Sanhedrin, the council that governed Jewish affairs under the Roman governor, who from AD 26 to 36 was Pontius Pilate. The officers sent to arrest Jesus (7:32, 45) were the temple guard, who served under the captain of the temple (Acts 4:1, 5:24-26) and kept order in its courts; they were probably Levites.

When John writes that people spoke of Jesus only in secret “for fear of the Jews” (7:13), the speakers are themselves Jews in Jerusalem, so the phrase must mean the authorities. John's word Ioudaioi can mean Judeans as distinct from Galileans, the Jewish people as a whole, or, as often in these chapters, the religious leadership in Jerusalem that opposed Jesus. Reading these texts as a judgment on the Jewish people has a long and shameful history in the church, and John's own narrative resists it. Jesus and his disciples are Jews keeping a Jewish feast; some of the crowd believe (7:31); the officers are moved (7:46); and a Pharisee, Nicodemus, insists on a fair hearing (7:51).

The Pharisees' contempt for “this crowd that does not know the law” (7:49) reflects a real social divide. Later rabbinic texts call the unlearned or careless common people the am ha-aretz, literally ‘people of the land’, and Hillel is remembered as saying that such a person cannot be truly pious (m. Avot 2:5). The remark about Galilee (7:52) belongs to the Judean view of Galilee as a provincial region far from the center of learning. It is also not quite accurate: the prophet Jonah came from Gath-hepher in Galilee (2 Kings 14:25), a few miles from Nazareth. The leaders' own claim fails the test of the Scriptures they tell Nicodemus to search.

Jesus' brothers (7:3-5), named in Mark 6:3 as James, Joses, Judas, and Simon, did not believe in him at this stage. After the resurrection they are among the believers in Jerusalem (Acts 1:14), Jesus appears to James (1 Corinthians 15:7), and James becomes a leader of the Jerusalem church (Acts 15:13, Galatians 2:9); Josephus records his execution in AD 62 (Antiquities 20.200). The unbelief of 7:5 is not the end of their story. Christians have understood the brothers as younger sons of Mary, as sons of Joseph by an earlier marriage, or as cousins; the text itself does not settle the question.
cultural:
The Feast of Tabernacles, or Booths (Hebrew Sukkot), was the great autumn pilgrimage festival, held for seven days from the fifteenth of the month Tishri, in September or October, with a closing assembly on the eighth day (Leviticus 23:33-43, Numbers 29:12-38, Deuteronomy 16:13-15). Families lived in temporary shelters of branches to remember Israel's wilderness years, and the feast gave thanks for the harvest of grapes and olives at the end of the dry season, just before the rains. Josephus calls it the holiest and greatest of the Jewish feasts (Antiquities 8.100), and it was so well known that it could be called simply the Feast. Every seventh year the law was read aloud to all Israel at this feast (Deuteronomy 31:10-13, Nehemiah 8:18), which gives an edge to Jesus' charge that no one keeps the law (7:19).

The Mishnah, compiled around AD 200 but describing the temple of this period, records two ceremonies. Each morning of the seven days a priest filled a golden flask holding three logs from the Pool of Siloam, carried it up to the temple to the sound of the shofar, and poured it out with wine at the altar through silver bowls (m. Sukkah 4:9). It was a prayer for the coming rains and a sign of hope. At night the Court of the Women was lit by great golden lamps, and the Mishnah says there was no courtyard in Jerusalem that did not reflect their light, while men of piety danced with torches and Levites sang (m. Sukkah 5:2-4). Whoever had not seen the rejoicing at the place of water-drawing, it says, had never seen rejoicing in his life (m. Sukkah 5:1). On the seventh day the priests circled the altar seven times with willow branches (m. Sukkah 4:5), and the Hallel psalms, including Psalm 118 with its cry “O LORD, save us”, were sung throughout. The name of the rejoicing came from Isaiah 12:3, “With joy you will draw water from the springs of salvation”, and the Jerusalem Talmud later explains that it was called the place of drawing because from there people drew the Holy Spirit (y. Sukkah 5:1). Zechariah 14, where living waters flow out from Jerusalem and the nations come up year after year to keep the Feast of Tabernacles (14:8, 16-19), became the prophetic reading for the feast, and Ezekiel's river flowing from the temple (Ezekiel 47:1-12) was connected with the water rite.

The crowd's arguments reflect real expectations. Many held that the Messiah would be a descendant of David from Bethlehem (Micah 5:2, 2 Samuel 7:12-16), and a Galilean seemed an unlikely candidate. Others believed the Messiah would be hidden until he appeared. The Similitudes of Enoch speak of the Son of Man hidden before God from before creation (1 Enoch 48:6), 4 Ezra says no one can see God's son until his day (4 Ezra 13:52), and in the second century Justin Martyr has his Jewish partner Trypho say that the Messiah, if he has been born, is unknown and has no power until Elijah comes to anoint him (Dialogue with Trypho 8.4). The question of whether the Messiah would do more signs than Jesus (7:31) presumes a messianic figure who works wonders, like the prophet like Moses. Jesus' learning “without having studied” (7:15) means he had no recognized teacher; a rabbi's authority normally came from the teacher under whom he trained, and the council later marvels that Peter and John are ‘unschooled’ (Acts 4:13). Jesus answers that his teacher is the one who sent him (7:16).

The argument about circumcision (7:22-23) follows a recognized rule. Circumcision on the eighth day (Leviticus 12:3), given first to Abraham (Genesis 17:10-12), was performed even when the eighth day fell on a Sabbath, and the Mishnah allows everything needed for it on that day (m. Shabbat 19:2) and praises circumcision because it overrides the Sabbath (m. Nedarim 3:11). The Babylonian Talmud later records Rabbi Eleazar ben Azariah reasoning that if circumcision, which concerns one member of the body, overrides the Sabbath, how much more does saving the whole body (b. Yoma 85b). Jesus uses the same kind of argument from the lesser to the greater. Nicodemus's appeal (7:51) also rests on the law, which required judges to hear both sides and investigate thoroughly (Deuteronomy 1:16-17, 17:4, 19:18).
literary:
The chapter is built from overheard voices. John records whispering (7:12, 32), questions, arguments, and verdicts from one group after another, so that the reader hears the city arguing about Jesus: he is a good man, he deceives the people, he has a demon, he is the Prophet, he is the Christ, he cannot be the Christ. Time markers structure it: before the feast in Galilee (7:1-9), the middle of the feast in Jerusalem (7:10-36), and the last day (7:37-52). Each section ends with a failed attempt to seize Jesus (7:30, 32, 44-45), and each failure is explained by his hour, not by human caution.

The theme of origin runs throughout, full of irony. The crowd says “we know where this man is from” (7:27); Jesus answers that they know his earthly origin but not the one who sent him (7:28-29). Some object that the Christ must come from Bethlehem (7:42), and John's readers, who know the tradition of Jesus' birth there recorded in Matthew and Luke, hear the irony. The Pharisees retort that no prophet comes from Galilee (7:52), a claim their own Scriptures contradict. Their question, “Have any of the rulers or Pharisees believed in Him?” (7:48), is answered at once by Nicodemus, one of their own. The theme of going away also runs through the chapter: the brothers want him to go up (7:3), he goes up in secret (7:10), and he says he is going to the one who sent him where they cannot come (7:33-34), which the hearers misunderstand as a trip to the Greek-speaking Diaspora (7:35). John's readers know that the message did in fact go to the Greeks.

The climax in 7:37-39 is carefully placed. Jesus stands and cries out, a posture of solemn proclamation, on the last and greatest day, and John adds an explanatory note, one of his asides to the reader, that the saying concerned the Spirit, to be given after Jesus was glorified. The verse numbering places 7:53 in this chapter, but that verse opens the account of the woman caught in adultery, which the earliest manuscripts lack; without it, 7:52 is followed directly by 8:12. See the note on chapter 8.

outline.t: Jesus' brothers urge him to go to the feast
Teaching in the temple: his teaching is from God
Where is he from, and where is he going?
The last day: rivers of living water
The officers return; Nicodemus asks for a hearing

doctrines.note: John explains Jesus' saying about living water: “He was speaking about the Spirit” (7:39). The Spirit would be given in the new way the prophets promised (Ezekiel 36:25-27, Joel 2:28) only after Jesus was glorified, that is, after his death, resurrection, and return to the Father. This prepares for the promises of the Spirit in chapters 14 to 16 and the gift in 20:22.

Jesus says his teaching is not his own but comes from the one who sent him, and that whoever wants to do God's will can recognize it (7:16-17). Knowing the truth about Jesus is tied to willingness to obey God, not only to intellectual inquiry, and the one who seeks the sender's glory rather than his own is shown to be true (7:18).

The crowd's arguments show how many expectations gathered around the Christ (the Anointed One, Hebrew Messiah): a son of David from Bethlehem, a figure of hidden origin, a worker of signs, the Prophet like Moses. John presents Jesus as fulfilling and surpassing all of them, and lets the reader see the irony in each objection.

Jesus defends his healing on the Sabbath (5:1-18) by the accepted practice of circumcising on the Sabbath (7:22-23). If the law allows one part of the body to be made whole on the Sabbath, it cannot forbid making the whole man well. The Sabbath is fulfilled, not broken, by the work of restoring life.

At the feast that poured water at the altar and read Ezekiel's river from the temple and Zechariah's living waters from Jerusalem, Jesus offers himself as the source of living water (7:37-38). What the temple and its rites looked for, God's life flowing out to his people and the nations, is now found in him.

words.note: Skēnopēgia, the Feast of Tabernacles or Booths, literally the pitching of tents. It occurs only here in the New Testament (7:2); the Greek Old Testament uses it for the feast in Deuteronomy 16:16 and 31:10 and in Zechariah 14:16-19, where the nations come up to keep it. John has already said that the Word ‘pitched his tent’ among us (1:14), using the related verb skēnoō, so setting these chapters at this feast is fitting.

Kairos, time, especially the right or appointed time, as distinct from chronos, time as duration, though the two often overlap. It occurs about 85 times in the New Testament but in John only here, three times (7:6, 8). Jesus tells his brothers that their time is always at hand but his has not yet come: for them any moment is as good as another; his life follows the Father's timing. John elsewhere uses hōra, hour, for the same appointed moment of the cross (7:30).

Gongysmos, murmuring or whispering, a low muttering of complaint or rumor. It occurs four times in the New Testament (7:12, Acts 6:1, Philippians 2:14, 1 Peter 4:9). The Greek Old Testament uses it for Israel's grumbling in the wilderness (Exodus 16:7-9), and the related verb was used of the crowd in 6:41. Here it describes a city talking under its breath about Jesus, afraid to speak openly (7:13).

Planaō, to lead astray, deceive, or cause to wander. It occurs about 39 times in the New Testament, twice in this chapter (7:12, 47). To call Jesus one who leads the people astray was a serious charge: Deuteronomy 13:1-5 commands death for a prophet who works signs but leads Israel after other gods. Later Jewish tradition preserved the charge that Jesus led Israel astray (b. Sanhedrin 43a), and Justin Martyr reports it too (Dialogue with Trypho 69.7).

Koilia, belly, womb, or inmost being, rendered “from within him” (7:38). It occurs about 22 times in the New Testament, in John only here and in 3:4, where Nicodemus asks about entering his mother's womb. In Hebrew thought the inner parts were the seat of the self. The Greek can be punctuated two ways, making either the believer or Christ the source of the streams; see the note on the text. Either way the water is the Spirit (7:39), and no single Old Testament verse matches the quotation exactly, so Jesus is probably gathering passages such as Isaiah 58:11, Ezekiel 47:1-12, and Zechariah 14:8, together with the water from the rock (Exodus 17:6, Psalm 78:15-16).

Schisma, a split or division, from the verb for tearing cloth (Mark 2:21). It occurs eight times in the New Testament, three of them in John, each time of people divided over Jesus (7:43, 9:16, 10:19). In 1 Corinthians it names factions within the church. John shows that Jesus' presence forces a decision and divides even a single crowd.

Diaspora, dispersion. It occurs three times in the New Testament (7:35, James 1:1, 1 Peter 1:1) and in the Greek Old Testament for Israel scattered among the nations (Deuteronomy 28:25, Isaiah 49:6, Psalm 147:2). By the first century far more Jews lived outside the land than in it, in Alexandria, Antioch, Rome, and across Asia Minor. The authorities mock the idea that Jesus would go and teach the Greeks, but John's readers know that the message did go to them (12:20-23).

christ:
At the festival that looked back to God's care in the wilderness and forward to living water flowing from Jerusalem, Jesus stands up and offers himself as the source of that water. In the wilderness God gave water from the rock (Exodus 17:6, Numbers 20:11, Psalm 78:15-16), and Paul would later say that the rock was Christ (1 Corinthians 10:4). The prophets promised that God would pour water on the thirsty and his Spirit on Israel's offspring (Isaiah 44:3), that he would put his Spirit within his people (Ezekiel 36:27), and that a river would flow from the temple to give life wherever it went (Ezekiel 47:9). Jesus claims to give what the feast prayed for and what the prophets promised, and John identifies it plainly as the Spirit. This extends the offer made to the Samaritan woman of water that becomes a spring welling up to eternal life (4:14), and it points to the cross, where blood and water flow from Jesus' side (19:34), and to Easter evening, when he breathes the Spirit on his disciples (20:22). The Spirit's coming depends on Jesus being glorified, which in John means his death, resurrection, and exaltation together (12:23-24).

The chapter also shows who Jesus is in relation to the Father. His teaching is from the one who sent him (7:16); he knows the Father because he is from him (7:29); he is going back to the one who sent him (7:33). His origin is not Nazareth or even Bethlehem but God. His brothers cannot hurry him and the officers cannot seize him, because his hour belongs to the Father. And the verdict of the temple officers, men sent to arrest him who came back with nothing but amazement, “Never has anyone spoken like this man!” (7:46), stands as the chapter's witness to him. Every expectation voiced in the crowd, Prophet, Christ, son of David, one whose origin is hidden, is true of him in a way the speakers did not understand.
interpretation:
The early church read 7:37-39 in two ways, depending on punctuation. The reading later called Eastern, found in Origen and followed by Athanasius and most Greek fathers, puts a full stop after drink and makes the believer the one from whom rivers flow. The reading called Western, associated with Justin, Irenaeus, Hippolytus, and Tertullian, runs ‘let the one who believes in me drink’ and makes Christ the source. Both readings have modern defenders, and English versions print one in the text and the other in a note. Augustine preached through the chapter in his Tractates on John 28-32, and John Chrysostom in his Homilies on John; both read the living water as the Spirit's gift to believers, as John's own note requires.

The saying about not going up to the feast (7:8) drew fire early. The pagan philosopher Porphyry, in the third century, used it to accuse Jesus of inconstancy, as Jerome reports (Against the Pelagians 2.17), and some copyists changed not to not yet. The question of the Messiah's origin (7:27, 41-42) became a set piece in Christian apologetics. Justin Martyr answered the Jewish expectation of a hidden Messiah (Dialogue with Trypho 8, 110), and interpreters have long seen in 7:42 an instance of John's irony, since his readers knew Jesus was born in Bethlehem. Nineteenth-century critics such as F. C. Baur instead took the verse as evidence that John knew nothing of the Bethlehem birth.

Modern scholarship has recovered the Tabernacles background. Commentators such as Raymond Brown (The Gospel According to John I-XII, 1966) and Craig Keener (The Gospel of John: A Commentary, 2003) set Jesus' words against the water and light ceremonies of m. Sukkah, and Brown organized chapters 5 to 10 around the feasts. Rudolf Bultmann (1941) rearranged the chapter's sections in the belief that its order had been disturbed, a proposal most later interpreters have not followed. Jewish scholars and the church's own reckoning with anti-Judaism have sharpened attention to John's Ioudaioi; the Second Vatican Council's declaration Nostra Aetate (1965) taught that the Jewish people should not be presented as rejected or accursed, and Adele Reinhartz, among others, has asked how chapters 7 and 8 have shaped Christian views of Jews.

In the liturgy the chapter belongs to Pentecost. The Byzantine lectionary reads John 7:37-52 with 8:12 on Pentecost Sunday, passing over the story of the adulteress, and the Orthodox feast of Mid-Pentecost, halfway between Easter and Pentecost, reads 7:14-30, where Jesus teaches in the temple in the middle of the feast; its icon shows the young Christ teaching the elders. The Roman Catholic Vigil of Pentecost reads 7:37-39, and the Revised Common Lectionary offers the same passage for the Day of Pentecost in Year A. The image of rivers of living water has passed into hymnody and into the church's prayer for the Spirit.
text:
Three places in this chapter show differences between English Bibles. In verse 8 the oldest papyri, Papyrus 66 and Papyrus 75, with Codex Vaticanus and many later manuscripts, read ‘I am not yet going up to this feast’, which the King James Version follows (‘I go not up yet’). Codex Sinaiticus, Codex Bezae, and others read ‘I am not going up’. Most modern editors print ‘not’ (as the BSB does), judging that ‘not yet’ is an early attempt to spare Jesus the charge of inconsistency, since the harder reading is more likely to have been softened than invented. Some modern scholars, noting how early the ‘not yet’ papyri are, think it original.

In verses 37 and 38 the question is punctuation, which the earliest manuscripts do not mark. The BSB, like most modern versions, reads “If anyone is thirsty, let him come to Me and drink. Whoever believes in Me, as the Scripture has said: ‘Streams of living water will flow from within him.’” Here the believer is the source of the streams. Many versions give in a note the alternative, ‘let the one who is thirsty come to me, and let the one who believes in me drink’, which makes the streams flow from Christ, which fits 19:34 and the rock in the wilderness. The Greek allows both.

In verse 39 the Greek says literally ‘the Spirit was not yet’, meaning not yet given in the way Jesus promises; some manuscripts, including Codex Vaticanus, add ‘given’, and others add ‘holy’ or ‘upon them’. The BSB supplies “given” as the sense requires. In verse 46 some manuscripts expand the officers' words; in verse 52 Papyrus 66 in its first hand reads ‘the Prophet’, turning the leaders' claim into a denial that the Prophet like Moses could come from Galilee. Verse 53 begins the story of the woman caught in adultery (7:53-8:11), which is absent from the earliest manuscripts and which modern Bibles mark with brackets or a note; the full textual history is given in the note on chapter 8.

teach.big: Jesus, whose time and origin are set by the Father, fulfills the feast's hope by offering himself as the source of the living water of the Spirit, and every attempt to judge him by appearances fails.

outline.t: Unbelief can live very close to Jesus, and he will not be managed by those who want him to perform on their schedule.
Fear of powerful people keeps many from speaking openly about Jesus even when they are curious.
Jesus' teaching comes from God, and a willingness to do God's will opens the way to recognizing it.
The Sabbath law itself shows that restoring a whole person honors God; stop judging by appearances.
People can know Jesus' earthly background and still not know where he comes from.
Jesus' going to the Father is a limit on those who reject him: a time comes when he cannot be found.
The thirsty are invited to come to Jesus and drink, and the gift he gives is the Spirit, poured out after his glorification.
Jesus divides crowds, and the objections raised against him often reveal what the objectors do not know.
Power can dismiss honest testimony and fair process, but truth keeps finding witnesses, even among the powerful.

teach.pitfalls:
One common misreading makes 7:37-39 a promise of emotional refreshment or spiritual experience detached from Jesus' cross; John ties the Spirit's coming to Jesus' glorification, and the living water flows from the crucified and risen Christ. Another uses 7:17 to suggest that anyone who does not believe must be unwilling to obey God, which turns an invitation into an accusation. The verse invites honest willingness; it does not diagnose every doubter.

Teachers should avoid presenting 7:8-10 as a model of clever evasion, and should not claim more certainty about the textual question than the evidence allows. They should also avoid reading the Jews of 7:1, 11, 13, and 35 as the Jewish people generally; in this chapter the crowd, the people of Jerusalem, and the authorities are distinguished, and Jesus and his followers are themselves Jews at a Jewish feast. Finally, 7:24, ‘stop judging by appearances’, is sometimes used to forbid all moral judgment; the same verse commands right judgment.
teach.pastoral: The chapter will speak to people whose own families do not share or respect their faith. Jesus' brothers did not believe in him, and he did not force them, yet at least one of them later led the church in Jerusalem. It will also speak to those who have been silenced by fear of powerful people, and to those who, like Nicodemus, raised a fair question and were mocked for it. Those who are spiritually dry, or who feel they have nothing left to give, should hear 7:37 as an invitation, not a demand: the thirsty are the ones called to come and drink.

hard.q: Did Jesus mislead his brothers when he said he was not going up to the feast and then went?
hard.a:
The objection is ancient. The pagan philosopher Porphyry, in the third century, pointed to 7:8-10 as proof that Jesus was inconsistent or untruthful, since he said he was not going up and then went, and Jerome records the charge (Against the Pelagians 2.17). Some early copyists felt the difficulty too: several manuscripts, including the early papyri 66 and 75 and Codex Vaticanus, read ‘not yet’ in place of ‘not’. Modern skeptical readers have taken the scene as one of several places where John's Jesus speaks in a way that is hard to square with plain truthfulness.

Interpreters answer in several ways. The first is textual: if ‘not yet’ is original, as a minority of scholars hold, the problem disappears. The second, held by many who accept ‘not’ as original, points to the reason Jesus gives, “My time has not yet come.” He refuses to go up on his brothers' terms, as a public display to win followers at their prompting (7:3-4), and he later goes privately, not as a pilgrim making himself known. On this view the present tense means ‘I am not going up now, in the way you propose’. The third, favored by a number of modern commentators, observes that in John going up (anabainō) can carry a double sense, since Jesus' final going up will be to the Father (20:17), and his time for that going up has not yet come. All of these readings agree on what the scene shows: Jesus refused to let his brothers set his timetable, and he acts only when the Father's time comes. Readers who hold that Jesus spoke truly find these explanations adequate; readers who do not will judge the scene by their prior view of the Gospel's reliability.

hard.q: Does John know that Jesus was born in Bethlehem, or does the crowd's objection count against it?
hard.a:
The objection runs like this. John never mentions Jesus' birth in Bethlehem or his descent from David. When the crowd objects that the Christ must come from David's line and from Bethlehem (7:42), and when the leaders say no prophet comes from Galilee (7:52), John offers no correction. Nineteenth-century critics such as F. C. Baur took this as evidence that the fourth evangelist either did not know or did not accept the birth stories of Matthew and Luke, and some modern scholars, including Rudolf Bultmann, held that John was indifferent to Jesus' earthly origin, since what mattered was that he came from God. Jewish readers have long noted that the objection was a fair one: Micah 5:2 and the promise to David set real expectations, and a Galilean teacher did not obviously fit them.

Others read the silence as irony, one of John's favorite techniques. C. K. Barrett (The Gospel According to St John, 1955), F. F. Bruce (The Gospel of John, 1983), and D. A. Carson (The Gospel According to John, 1991) argue that John expects his readers to know the tradition and lets the crowd condemn itself: they are sure Jesus cannot be the Christ because he comes from Galilee, when in fact he was born in Bethlehem, and more deeply, comes from the Father. John uses the same device in 7:27 and in 11:50, where Caiaphas prophesies without knowing it. On this reading the evangelist does not correct the objection because the correction is the joke the reader is meant to catch. Scholars also note that John is primarily concerned with Jesus' heavenly origin (7:28-29, 8:23), so that the question of Bethlehem, true or not, cannot settle who he is. Readers should know that John's text itself does not decide between these views; the Bethlehem tradition rests on Matthew 2 and Luke 2.

observe: What do Jesus' brothers urge him to do, and what reason does John give for their urging?
What different opinions about Jesus do the crowds, the people of Jerusalem, and the Pharisees express in this chapter?
What does Jesus cry out on the last day of the feast, and how does John explain it?
interpret: Why does Jesus say that anyone who wants to do God's will will know whether his teaching is from God? How are obedience and understanding connected?
What is the irony in the crowd's objection that the Christ must come from Bethlehem, and in the leaders' claim that no prophet comes from Galilee?
Why does John say the Spirit had not yet been given because Jesus had not yet been glorified?
apply: Jesus' own brothers did not believe in him. What does it mean for you that unbelief can live so close to Jesus, and that it need not be the end of the story?
Where are you tempted to judge someone by appearances rather than justly, as Nicodemus asked the council not to do?
Jesus invites the thirsty to come to him and drink. What are you thirsty for, and where have you been trying to satisfy it?
